## Getting started

High-frequency processing is everything that turns raw sonic-anemometer and gas-analyzer records into a 30-minute flux. The building blocks you may know from CO₂ still apply: coordinate rotation, time-lag correction, detrending or high-pass filtering, air-density (WPL) terms where needed, spectral corrections, and quality flags. CH₄ and N₂O change the emphasis because the signal is often weaker and more intermittent.

::: {.icos-box}
For the full system-setup specification (sensors, inlet geometry, calibration, maintenance), see the [ICOS CH₄/N₂O instruction](https://www.europe-fluxdata.eu/icos/documents/instructions/eddych4n2o) and [Nemitz et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1515/intag-2017-0042). Raw-data processing for CO₂ and energy fluxes is covered in Sabbatini et al. (2018), [doi:10.1515/intag-2017-0043](https://doi.org/10.1515/intag-2017-0043). This page covers the issues that most often surprise people new to non-CO₂ fluxes.
:::

## Instruments and setup

These are complementary notes, not a sensor list.

- **Closed-path laser spectrometers** are widely used for both CH₄ and N₂O. Pay attention to tube length, flow rate, and how you will find the time lag relative to the sonic anemometer.
- **Open-path CH₄ analyzers** (including the LI-COR LI-7700) involve a well-known trade-off: open-path systems need larger air-density corrections, while closed-path systems can lose high-frequency signal in the tube under some conditions. See Detto et al. (2011), *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*, [doi:10.1016/j.agrformet.2011.05.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2011.05.014).
- **Network rules come first.** As a matter of ICOS network policy, ICOS no longer accepts the LI-7700 at ICOS Class 1 ecosystem stations. If you are part of ICOS, follow ICOS. If you are not, treat instrument choice as a scientific and practical decision, follow your own network's rules, and document your reasoning. This site does not ban any commercial sensor.
- **Record what you will need later:** gas mole fractions, the three wind components, sonic temperature, and the diagnostics your analyzer provides (signal strength, flow, cell or mirror status, and so on).

## Time lag

For closed-path systems, detecting the time delay between the sonic anemometer and the analyzer is one of the most important high-frequency steps, especially when fluxes are small. When the signal-to-noise ratio is low, a lag search over a wide window tends to lock onto noise and can bias fluxes. Langford et al. (2015), *Atmospheric Measurement Techniques*, [doi:10.5194/amt-8-4197-2015](https://doi.org/10.5194/amt-8-4197-2015), is a good introduction to time-lag determination and detection limits for low signal-to-noise eddy-covariance data.

Points emphasized in committee discussions:

- Detect time lags carefully for closed-path laser spectrometers.
- Use a **predetermined, relatively narrow lag-search window** together with a **default (nominal) lag**, rather than letting the search wander over a wide window at every interval.
- **High-pass filtered lag correction**, as implemented in [eddy4R](https://github.com/NEONScience/eddy4R), is one documented approach.

## Wavelets and data retention

Conventional stationarity and turbulence flags can remove a large fraction of CH₄ or N₂O records at sites where fluxes arrive in short events. Wavelet-based methods are being used in this community to retain more high-quality data and to identify disruptive events, without treating every non-stationary period as unusable. Think of wavelets as a promising and actively used approach, not a required standard.

## Despiking, spectral corrections, and quality flags

- **Despiking.** Remove physically impossible spikes in the raw data before averaging, but be careful not to treat real emission pulses (ebullition, fertilizer bursts) as noise.
- **Spectral corrections.** These can become large when tubes, filters, or analyzers attenuate high frequencies. Intervals with extreme correction factors are often filtered later, at the [half-hourly stage](half-hourly.qmd).
- **Quality flags.** Standard flux quality flags, such as the Mauder and Foken (2004) scheme based on steady-state and integral-turbulence-characteristics (SSITC) tests, are still commonly applied. Many groups keep quality classes 0 and 1 for quantitative work.

## Software people use at this stage

[EddyPro](https://www.licor.com/products/eddy-covariance/software) (LI-COR; the [processing engine is open source](https://github.com/LI-COR-Environmental/eddypro-engine)) is the processing software most widely used in this community to compute 30-minute fluxes from raw files. Other groups use in-house MATLAB, R, or Python code, or research pipelines such as [eddy4R](https://github.com/NEONScience/eddy4R).

Whatever you choose, **write down your settings**: the lag window and nominal lag, the despiking method, the spectral corrections, and whether a default CO₂-style outlier filter was left on.

## A short high-frequency checklist

- [ ] Confirm clock synchronization between the sonic anemometer and the gas analyzer (see ICOS for recommended practice).
- [ ] For closed-path systems, document the inlet position relative to the sonic anemometer, the tube length, and the flow rate.
- [ ] Set a physically plausible lag-search window and a nominal lag.
- [ ] Inspect lag detections on days with clear fluxes *and* on days with near-zero fluxes.
- [ ] Review raw-data diagnostics (signal strength, flow, analyzer warnings) before you trust a long automated run.
- [ ] Record software versions and processing settings so the 30-minute product is reproducible.
